lines.text: There is a room I still think about.
It smelled of cardamom and old books.
The window faced west, and in the afternoons, everything went gold.
I didn't know it wouldn't always be like this.
We used to eat dinner with the radio on.
My mother would dance between the stove and the table.
Badly. Wonderfully badly.
The whole house felt warm.
The summer I turned seventeen, we moved.
She said it was necessary.
I carried my things down the stairs in boxes.
I didn't look back.
The arguments started that winter.
Small things at first.
A door held too long.
A silence that lasted days.
Then bigger things.
I stood in the hallway one night, not moving.
Barely breathing.
The night it ended, there was rain.
There were voices and then there was nothing.
A door.
A car.
Headlights disappearing down the street.
I sat on the floor of the empty hallway.
For months after, I woke at three in the morning.
Smaller. Colder.
I learned to make my own tea.
I learned to sit with the silence without fighting it.
But slowly, the way light comes back after winter without you noticing, things began to feel possible again.
I found her letters in a drawer.
Her handwriting was terrible.
The last letter said: don't take any of this too seriously.
It's just a life. Make it yours.
I laughed out loud when I read that.
Because it was exactly what she would say.
I opened all the windows that morning.
I made cardamom tea.
I put on music and I danced badly and wonderfully badly.
The room at the end of the hall is gone now.
But I carry it.
And on certain afternoons, when everything goes gold, I feel it again.
Right here.
